section_summary: This section documents U.S. debates over restricting exports to Japan, especially aviation gasoline, petroleum technology, aircraft-grade alloys, lead, molybdenum, steel, and other strategic materials. It combines public petitions against aiding Japanese aggression in China with corporate requests for guidance and State Department efforts to administer a voluntary “moral embargo.” The section also records congressional inquiries, diplomatic reporting, and disputes over existing contracts between American companies and Japanese industrial concerns.

subfiles.title: White House referral to the State Department
subfiles.about: Refers correspondence concerning Japan-related trade policy to the State Department.
subfiles.summary: The White House respectfully refers an unspecified communication to the State Department for consideration. The sheet is signed by Edwin M. Watson as Secretary to the President.

subfiles.title: Senator Murray forwards Wong Sun's letter
subfiles.about: Forwards a constituent's appeal to President Roosevelt and requests confirmation of its receipt.
subfiles.summary: Senator Murray encloses a letter to the President from his constituent Wong Sun. He asks General Watson to acknowledge that the letter reached the White House.

subfiles.title: Wong Sun appeal against war-supply sales to Japan
subfiles.about: Asks the President to prevent sales of war supplies to Japan and avoid trade arrangements harmful to China.
subfiles.summary: Wong Sun condemns Japanese attacks on defenseless Chinese civilians and appeals to Roosevelt's humanitarian sympathies. He asks the President to stop war-supply sales and oppose any trade treaty with Japan that might harm China.

subfiles.title: State Department acknowledgment to Senator Murray
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Murray's transmittal of Wong Sun's letter concerning war supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hull acknowledges the White House referral of Murray's letter and Wong Sun's enclosed appeal. He thanks Murray and indicates that new legislation would be required for the requested export restrictions.

subfiles.title: White House referral of Washington Committee correspondence
subfiles.about: Refers a communication to State Department officials for attention and consideration.
subfiles.summary: The White House sends the accompanying correspondence to the State Department. The referral bears Watson's name and was routed to Stanley K. Hornbeck.

subfiles.title: Washington Committee for Aid to China policy appeal
subfiles.from: Mortimer Graves, Washington Committee for Aid to China
subfiles.about: Urges stronger American action against Japanese aggression and American exports supporting it.
subfiles.summary: The committee argues that American opinion is ready for executive leadership against Japanese aggression in China. It requests nonrecognition of the Wang Ching-wei regime, postponement of a new commercial treaty, termination of war-material shipments, and a major loan to the Chinese Industrial Cooperatives. It presents these measures as necessary to restore American integrity and avoid strengthening Japanese militarists.

subfiles.title: Reply to Mortimer Graves
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the committee's letter on Far Eastern policy.
subfiles.summary: The Department acknowledges receipt through the White House of Graves's communication. It states that the committee's views have been carefully noted and appreciated.
keywords: Washington Committee for Aid to China

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on molybdenum producers' export restraint
subfiles.from: Great Britain despatch attributed to Johnson
subfiles.about: References information that American molybdenum producers agreed temporarily not to export to Russia or Japan.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to an original paper in file 841.5151/1488. It records that Butterworth conveyed to the American Embassy in Paris an agreement by American producers to suspend molybdenum exports to Russia and Japan.

subfiles.title: Senate forwarding memorandum concerning Samuel Wilson
subfiles.about: Forwards a constituent's inquiry for consideration and requests return of the letter.
subfiles.summary: Senator Davis submits an enclosed communication to the chief of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs. He asks that its request be handled and the original returned after disposition.

subfiles.title: Samuel Wilson inquiry about Japanese scrap buyers
subfiles.about: Seeks contacts with Japanese Government fiscal agents for clients wishing to sell scrap.
subfiles.summary: Wilson says clients in the junk business want a direct connection with Japanese Government fiscal agents. He notes substantial shipments through San Francisco and says his clients could supply several carloads.

subfiles.title: Reply to Senator Davis on Japanese fiscal agents
subfiles.about: Reports that the Department has no record of Japanese fiscal agents purchasing the requested material in the United States.
subfiles.summary: The Department acknowledges Davis's inquiry on behalf of Samuel Wilson's clients. It says it knows of no Japanese Government fiscal agents in the country for this kind of purchasing and returns Wilson's original letter after retaining a copy.

subfiles.title: Ethyl Gasoline Corporation report on tetraethyl lead shipments
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, attention Charles W. Yost
subfiles.about: Reports the quantity of British-associated ethyl fluid and tetraethyl lead shipped to Japan in 1939.
subfiles.summary: The corporation reports that Associated Ethyl shipped 1,106,490 pounds of ethyl fluid containing 679,500 pounds of tetraethyl lead to Japan between May and December 1939. It states that no 1940 shipments had occurred and promises notification and monthly reporting of future shipments.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Associated Ethyl shipment report
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the report on Associated Ethyl's 1939 shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost thanks the company for its shipment figures and assumes the material was exported from the United States. He notes the arrangements for notifying the Department and submitting monthly reports.

subfiles.title: Frank Howard report on proposed Manchukuo ethyl plant
subfiles.about: Seeks approval for handling Associated Ethyl negotiations over a proposed plant in Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: Howard reports that Associated Ethyl is discussing an ethyl-process plant in Manchukuo but does not intend to finalize an agreement immediately. He says the American shareholders regard the moral embargo as applicable and suggests continuing discussions only on the understanding that no agreement can be completed until the embargo is lifted.

subfiles.title: State Department reply on Manchukuo plant negotiations
subfiles.about: Approves Howard's cautious approach as consistent with the moral-embargo policy.
subfiles.summary: Yost expresses appreciation for Howard's efforts to extend observance of the December 20 policy. Based on the information supplied, he finds the proposed procedure consistent with that policy and presumes British policy to be similar.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Japanese protest against aircraft moral embargo
subfiles.about: References a Japanese protest that the American aircraft moral embargo violated the 1911 treaty.
subfiles.summary: The sheet summarizes objections to the State Department's July 1, 1938 circular to aircraft manufacturers. The Japanese Embassy argued that the American position derogated from provisions of the 1911 treaty.

subfiles.title: Consular despatch on lead loaded aboard Akagi Maru
subfiles.about: Investigates Mexican lead loaded aboard the Japanese vessel Akagi Maru at Brownsville.
subfiles.summary: The consul reports that roughly 2,000 tons of ASARCO lead were loaded at Brownsville and reviews the production and markets of the two major Monterrey refineries. Because wartime conditions reduced European outlets, much recent Mexican lead had gone to Japan and other markets. The despatch concludes that the Brownsville lead was probably refined by American Smelting & Refining in Monterrey, while the origin of nearby scrap iron and steel remained unknown.

subfiles.title: A. Frasse inquiry about aircraft-alloy exports
subfiles.from: J. E. Lennon, A. Frasse & Co.
subfiles.about: Requests guidance on selling aircraft-grade alloy sheets and tubing through Volkart Brothers for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Frasse encloses Volkart Brothers' solicitation involving materials used in aircraft parts. The firm asks whether accepting such business would accord with the State Department's legal and moral policies.

subfiles.title: Volkart Brothers proposal for Japanese alloy sales
subfiles.about: Proposes marketing chromium-molybdenum and chromium-nickel-molybdenum products in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Volkart states that its Japanese affiliate is interested in alloy sheets and tubing used by the aircraft industry. It offers access to Japanese buyers, including government offices, and proposes discussions with a visiting representative.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to A. Frasse
subfiles.about: Advises that the proposed aircraft-alloy export transaction would conflict with announced policy.
subfiles.summary: The Department acknowledges Frasse's inquiry about sheets and tubing intended for Japan's aircraft industry. Citing the December 15 press release covering aeronautical equipment and materials essential to airplane manufacture, it concludes that the proposed sale would be inconsistent with policy.

subfiles.title: Universal Oil Products appointment confirmation
subfiles.about: Confirms a meeting with Green at which Gustav Egloff will also be present.
subfiles.summary: Halle confirms the parties' recent conversation and schedules an appointment for February 6. He states that Universal Oil Products research director Dr. Egloff will accompany him.

subfiles.title: Shell Oil interim acknowledgment
subfiles.from: R. I. Lewis, Shell Oil Company
subfiles.about: Reports a delay in compiling requested shipment information.
subfiles.summary: Shell acknowledges the Department's December 19 request. It expects to complete the requested information at the beginning of the following week.

subfiles.title: Shell Oil report on high-octane gasoline shipments
subfiles.about: Reports Shell's 1939 and early 1940 high-octane aviation-gasoline shipments to Japan and the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: Shell reports no relevant shipments from Gulf refineries and none from Pacific refineries to the Soviet Union. It details a 1939 shipment of 34,240 drums to Japan and a final 1940 consignment of 20,760 drums sold through Mitsui for the Japanese Navy. The company promises to report future inquiries or contemplated sales.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Shell aviation-gasoline report
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Shell's report and promise to disclose future sales.
subfiles.summary: The Department thanks Shell for its information on aviation-gasoline exports to Japan. It specifically notes the company's undertaking to report future transactions.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Congressman Celler about Japan Gasoline Company
subfiles.about: Records Celler's request for relief from the moral embargo's effect on a Japanese petroleum-technology contract.
subfiles.summary: Celler called for his friend, former Congressman Cohen, whose financial interest in Japan Gasoline Company was harmed by suspension of a Universal Oil Products contract. He proposed a conference among the interested parties. Ballantine and Moseley explained that Halle would soon consult Green and agreed to bring Celler's approach to Green's attention.

subfiles.title: Summary of Universal Oil Products contracts with Japan Gasoline Company
subfiles.about: Summarizes contracts, payments, plant orders, and arguments for exempting existing petroleum-technology work from the moral embargo.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum describes a 1928 patent-transfer contract and a 1938 expansion covering isooctane and other petroleum processes, for which Japan Gasoline Company paid $700,000. It identifies pending work for Mitsubishi Oil, Nippon Oil, the Miike plant, Toyo Shoko Oil, and Chosen Oil. It argues that the contracts predated the expanded embargo, that Japan already possessed much of the information, and that Universal should be allowed either to complete the whole contract or at least three advanced projects.

subfiles.title: Duplicate memorandum of conversation with Congressman Celler
subfiles.about: Duplicate record of Celler's intervention concerning the Universal Oil Products contract.
subfiles.summary: This copy repeats the account of Celler's appeal on behalf of former Congressman Cohen. It records discussion of a possible conference and Halle's forthcoming consultation with Green.

subfiles.title: Second duplicate memorandum of conversation with Congressman Celler
subfiles.about: A further copy of the memorandum concerning Celler and the suspended petroleum-technology contract.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum again describes Celler's concern over Cohen's investment and his request to convene the interested parties. Ballantine undertook to refer the matter to Green after Green's meeting with Halle.

subfiles.title: Green memorandum opposing an exception for Universal Oil Products
subfiles.about: Recommends denying any exception to the common suspension of aviation-gasoline technology contracts.
subfiles.summary: Green recalls that oil and engineering firms jointly agreed on December 14 to suspend existing contracts and new negotiations involving aviation-gasoline plants or technical information. Because Universal Oil Products accepted that arrangement, he argues that an exception would violate policy and undermine equal treatment among cooperating companies. He recommends telling Celler that no exception can be made.

subfiles.title: Green memorandum on calls with Celler and Halle
subfiles.about: Records telephone conversations confirming that no exception would be granted and that Universal intended to comply.
subfiles.summary: Green told Celler that every participating company had agreed to stop providing high-quality aviation-gasoline information to the affected countries. Celler said he understood but might return with Cohen. Halle separately reported that Celler, Cohen, and three Japanese representatives had pressed him to seek an exception, which he categorically refused to do.

subfiles.title: Chongqing Embassy despatch on proposed embargo petition
subfiles.from: Willys R. Peck, American Embassy, Chongqing
subfiles.about: Explains the Embassy's refusal to transmit a public petition demanding an embargo on munitions exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Peck encloses McCurdy's letter, the petition, and the Embassy's reply. He argues that the petition's accusation of American participation in Japanese aggression omitted the United States' opposition to Japan's invasion and could inflame Chinese hostility toward Americans. He asks the Department to approve the Embassy's refusal to become associated with the proposed publication.

subfiles.title: McCurdy request to cable the Chongqing petition
subfiles.about: Requests that the Embassy cable an embargo petition signed by American residents to Washington.
subfiles.summary: McCurdy says approximately twenty-five American citizens in Chongqing support the petition and that nobody approached had refused. He asks the Embassy to forward it promptly so its contents can be released to local newspapers while withholding three signers' names.

subfiles.title: Petition by American citizens in Chongqing
subfiles.to: President, Congress, and people of the United States
subfiles.about: Demands an immediate end to transactions supplying Japan's war effort.
subfiles.summary: The petition asserts that the United States had facilitated Japanese aggression in China by supplying the sinews of war. It argues that termination of the commercial treaty made cessation possible and appeals for immediate action against such transactions.

subfiles.title: List of attendees at the Chongqing International Club meeting
subfiles.about: Lists foreign and Chinese attendees associated with the meeting that produced the embargo appeal.
subfiles.summary: The page names missionaries, teachers, journalists, banking personnel, aviation personnel, and other residents who attended the meeting. It also provides Chinese names or occupational annotations for many attendees and separately identifies Chinese participants.

subfiles.title: Embassy reply declining to transmit McCurdy's petition
subfiles.about: Declines to transmit the petition because publication would imply official American association with a partial statement.
subfiles.summary: Peck infers that the petitioners intend to publicize both the appeal and its transmission through official channels. He refuses because the statement covers only one aspect of American Far Eastern policy and might harm friendship between Americans and Chinese.

subfiles.title: Congressman Hall forwards constituent petition
subfiles.about: Forwards a petition from constituents concerned about war-material shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hall sends Hull a petition addressed to the Secretary of State. He explains that he has told each constituent that their names and concerns would be forwarded to the Department.

subfiles.title: Hull acknowledgment to Congressman Hall
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of the petition opposing war-material shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hull confirms receipt of Hall's letter and its enclosed petition. He thanks Hall for forwarding the communication.

subfiles.title: Christopher Graham letter enclosing a contribution
subfiles.about: Encloses a fifty-dollar check connected with opposition to Japanese aggression in China.
subfiles.summary: Graham sends a brief handwritten communication and a fifty-dollar check intended for the American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression. He says he does not wish to embarrass the President and expresses confidence in presidential judgment.

subfiles.title: Return of Christopher Graham's check
subfiles.about: Returns Graham's check because the Department does not act as a transmitting agency for private donations.
subfiles.summary: Yost acknowledges Graham's letter and the check for the American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression. He explains that Graham can send it directly, returns the enclosure, and notes that federal law does not restrict contributions of this kind.

subfiles.title: Methodist petition for an embargo on war materials to Japan
subfiles.from: Members and friends of Methodist churches in the Portlandville–Oneonta area
subfiles.about: Condemns Japanese atrocities in China and urges legislation stopping American war-material exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The petition describes the bombing of Chinese cities, the Nanjing atrocities, and other violence committed by Japanese forces. It argues that American exports made the United States partly responsible and that termination of the 1911 treaty created an opportunity to change course. Signers from several Methodist congregations call for immediate legislation to end shipments of basic war materials to the aggressor nation.

subfiles.title: Japanese Chamber of Commerce request for export-control list
subfiles.from: Tatsuo Ono, Japanese Chamber of Commerce of New York
subfiles.about: Requests a complete list of commodities restricted or discouraged for sale or export to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The chamber asks which goods fall under the moral embargo or conservation controls on national resources. It seeks clear guidance on prohibited or restricted trade with Japan.

subfiles.title: Reply to Japanese Chamber of Commerce
subfiles.to: Japanese Chamber of Commerce of New York
subfiles.about: Supplies policy documents on aeronautical goods and strategic materials.
subfiles.summary: Yost encloses relevant State Department press releases and Army and Navy Munitions Board statements. He explains that the measures apply generally to countries engaged in unprovoked aerial attacks on civilians or to exports of designated strategic materials.

subfiles.title: Justice Department referral of Henry Stimson correspondence
subfiles.about: Forwards copies of Henry L. Stimson's letter and enclosure on American Far Eastern policy.
subfiles.summary: Rogge sends the State Department a photostatic copy of Stimson's January 25 letter and its enclosure. He states that Stimson has been informed of the referral.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Hamilton Fish on Japanese high-octane gasoline production
subfiles.about: Records Fish's request for authoritative information on Japan's ability to manufacture high-octane gasoline.
subfiles.summary: Fish says he has debated Upton Close over whether Japan possesses suitable factories and refineries. Hamilton replies that Japan buys substantial American supplies but that the more important question concerns access to technical production processes. He promises further inquiry through available diplomatic and commercial channels.

subfiles.title: Yost memorandum on Japanese aviation-gasoline capacity
subfiles.about: Summarizes limited intelligence on Japan's ability to produce aviation-gasoline blending agents.
subfiles.summary: Yost reports that Japan has a small number of plants producing blending agents but cannot meet more than a fraction of its aviation requirements. He characterizes Japanese processes as outdated and unable to produce the highest grades used by the American Army and Navy.

subfiles.title: Follow-up conversation with Hamilton Fish
subfiles.about: Provides Fish with production intelligence and American export figures for aviation gasoline.
subfiles.summary: Ballantine explains that Japanese production data are guarded as military secrets but that Japan's few plants are inadequate and technologically outdated. He reports 1939 American exports of 513,411 barrels to Japan, 65,937 to Kwantung, and 113,000 to China. Fish emphasizes that Japan could expand its plants or obtain processes from Germany or Russia, while Ballantine points to continued import dependence.

subfiles.title: Confidential instruction to the American Ambassador in Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits memoranda of the Hamilton Fish conversations for confidential information.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary encloses copies of the January 11 and January 15 conversations with Hamilton Fish. Both concern whether Japan manufactures high-octane gasoline.

subfiles.title: Triplicate memorandum on Senator Byrnes's export-statistics request
subfiles.to: Charles W. Yost and Joseph C. Green
subfiles.about: Records Byrnes's request for figures on war-material exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Byrnes asks for export figures covering war materials shipped to Japan during the preceding six months. Peurifoy tells Byrnes's secretary that the Department can provide only figures for arms, ammunition, and implements of war defined by the May 1, 1937 proclamation. He agrees to send the latest press release by special messenger.

subfiles.title: Camden Forge inquiry about turbine and pinion shafts
subfiles.about: Requests guidance before accepting a Japanese order for nickel-chrome-molybdenum steel shafts.
subfiles.summary: Camden Forge is considering a contract for turbine and pinion shafts for export to Japan. It asks whether a future embargo might cover the products and whether pre-embargo contracts could still be completed and shipped.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Camden Forge
subfiles.about: Explains the absence of current statutory authority for a general Japan embargo and supplies relevant policy statements.
subfiles.summary: Yost states that no existing statute authorizes a general embargo on exports to Japan and that new legislation would be necessary. He cannot predict congressional action. He encloses statements on strategic materials, aeronautical equipment, and materials essential to airplane manufacture.

subfiles.title: Green memorandum on Braden Copper molybdenum sale
subfiles.about: Records Kennecott representatives' explanation of a proposed Chilean molybdenum sale to Japanese interests.
subfiles.summary: Judge Covington and Carl Ulrich explain that Braden Copper, Kennecott's Chilean subsidiary, has received a Japanese order for seventy-five tons of molybdenum. They fear refusal could provoke Chilean intervention and broader government control over exports. Green notes that Chilean shipments fall outside the stated American policy and that Braden's total output would equal only about one-sixth of Japan's annual American purchases.

subfiles.title: Duplicate memorandum on Braden Copper molybdenum sale
subfiles.about: Duplicate record of the proposed sale of Chilean molybdenum to Japanese buyers.
subfiles.summary: The duplicate repeats Kennecott's argument that Braden Copper should accept the seventy-five-ton order to avoid Chilean governmental intervention. It also repeats the production estimate of seventy to ninety tons monthly and the comparison with Japan's larger purchases from the United States.

subfiles.title: Inland Steel telegram on proposed Japanese sale
subfiles.from: J. L. Block, Inland Steel Company
subfiles.about: Requests immediate guidance on negotiations to sell up to 100,000 tons of semifinished steel to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Block reports negotiations involving between fifty thousand and one hundred thousand tons of semifinished steel. He asks whether the State Department has any wishes in the matter and requests a same-day telegraphic response.

subfiles.title: State Department letter to J. L. Block
subfiles.about: Follows the Department's telegram with policy statements relevant to the proposed steel sale.
subfiles.summary: The Department refers to Block's telegram and its telegraphic reply. It encloses the December 15 and December 20 statements concerning aeronautical equipment and materials essential to airplane manufacture for countries whose forces attack civilian populations from the air.
